read: full: abstract, sections 1-5 (pp. 1-10), Appendix A.1, A.2.5-A.2.9 and A.3.2-A.3.4 (grading prompts, human check of the grader, settings; pp. 13, 20-26); skimmed the worked examples A.2.1-A.2.4 and the error-mode examples A.4 (pp. 13-19, 27-32)
venue_now: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2410.09988v2 of 13 Dec 2024, headed 'A PREPRINT' and dated October 2024 (p1). The text shows no venue, so the May entry 'arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.09988' matches this file.
what_it_is: HARDMath is a dataset of graduate-level applied-mathematics problems, inspired by a graduate course on asymptotic methods, that need analytical approximation (dominant balance, Laplace's method) rather than exact solution (pp. 1-4). Problems and their step-by-step worked solutions are generated by code (SymPy, SciPy) from randomly drawn coefficients, functional forms and initial conditions, and a problem is kept only if its approximate solution is within 10% of a numerically computed ground truth (pp. 2, 4-5). It holds 1,466 problems: 1,060 in a development set, 366 in the evaluation set HARDMATH-MINI and 40 hand-written word problems in applied-science contexts (pp. 1, 4). Answers are checked automatically (boxed answer, SymPy equivalence and numerical evaluation) and, for three of the four problem classes, also graded by GPT-4o against the answer key with rubrics adapted from course grading guidelines, for partial credit (p7, p25). Five models are evaluated; the best, o1-mini with 5-shot chain-of-thought, reaches 62.3% and GPT-4 43.8% (pp. 7-8).
domain: graduate-level applied mathematics (asymptotic and approximation methods for polynomials, nonlinear ODEs and integrals); 40 word problems set in applied-science contexts
size: 1,466 problems: 1,060 (development set) + 366 (HARDMATH-MINI, the evaluation set) + 40 word problems (pp. 1, 4, 10); seven problem types in four classes (p3); five models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, o1-mini, Llama3-8b, CodeLlama-13b) in 12 model-prompt settings (pp. 7-8)
source_of_items: generated from templates: code draws coefficients, degrees, functional forms, bounds and initial conditions at random and solves each problem algorithmically (pp. 2, 4, 13-20); the 40 word problems are hand-written (pp. 4, 6). A pilot of LLM-written physics contexts for 30 ODE problems is described but is not part of the evaluation (p6).
instances: generated (by code, 'no duplicate problems are included', p4); the evaluation set HARDMATH-MINI is a fixed released sample of 366, and the code 'can be used to generate any number of additional problems' (pp. 2, 6, 10)
has_gold_traces: yes: every problem comes with a code-generated LaTeX step-by-step solution embedded in explanatory text, final answers boxed (pp. 2, 4-5; examples pp. 13-21). The steps were not hand-checked ('manually verifying each solution step-by-step is impractical', p5), only the final result against a numerical ground truth, and the gold steps are not used to score model steps (p25).
evaluation: final answer (boxed answer compared by SymPy equivalence and numerical evaluation, p7) plus an LLM judge: GPT-4o grades Roots, ODEs and Integrals against the answer key with per-type rubrics, giving partial credit per solution regime, and for Laplace integrals half credit for reaching an intermediate checkpoint (p7, Table 5 p25). The paper calls this 'procedural grading' and says intermediate steps need grading (p7), but no individual step of a model's solution is scored.
human_validation: Items: the automatic gate keeps a problem only if its approximation is within 10% of the numerical ground truth (p5); HARDMATH-MINI is also checked by plotting analytical against numerical solutions for visual human verification (pp. 5, 13), and the conclusion calls the 366 MINI items and the 40 word problems 'human-verified' (p10). Evaluator: the authors 'manually verify a subset of grading responses' and find the LLM grading 'closely aligned with human grading' (p7); Table 6 gives the average human adjustment per model and problem type, from -0.15 to +0.07 points (p26). The size of the subset and any agreement statistic are not reported.
contamination_measures: none stated. The generator can produce new problems in any number (pp. 2, 10), but the paper presents this as scalability, not as a defence against contamination, and evaluates on a fixed public set.

engtrace_use.sentence: In mathematics, benchmarks ranging from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) to HardMath (Fan et al., 2024), Putnam-Axiom (Gulati et al., 2024), and GSM-Symbolic (Mirzadeh et al., 2024) rigorously test abstract logical deduction and reasoning stability. (S-M1; S-M3 then says abstract deduction does not transfer to reasoning under physical constraints)
engtrace_use.explanation: For HARDMath the characterisation is the reverse of the paper's own aim. HARDMath sets itself against datasets that 'focus on abstract, formal mathematics' (p2), targets approximate solutions 'that cannot be formalized using tools like Lean' (pp. 2-3), and draws its problems from those 'commonly encountered in real-world scientific and engineering contexts' that need computational tools and 'subjective judgment' (p1); its 40 word problems are set in applied-science contexts (pp. 1, 6, 8). It does not test reasoning stability: there is no perturbation or variance analysis (pp. 6-9). The sentence also omits what matters most for EngTrace: HARDMath already generates problems and step-by-step solutions by code with a numerical validity gate (pp. 2, 4-5) and grades with a rubric-based LLM judge for partial credit (p7), which makes it the nearest mathematics precedent for EngTrace's generated instances with gold solutions. Using it in S-M3 as an example of abstract mathematics that fails to transfer to physical constraints is not supported by the paper.

suggested_wording: HARDMath (Fan et al., 2024) generates graduate-level applied-mathematics problems (asymptotic approximation of polynomial roots, nonlinear ODEs and integrals) together with step-by-step solutions by code, keeps a problem only if its approximation lies within 10% of a numerical ground truth, and grades answers automatically and with a rubric-based GPT-4o grader for partial credit.
facts_to_cite: 1,466 problems inspired by a graduate course on asymptotic methods: 1,060 in the development set, 366 in the evaluation set HARDMATH-MINI and 40 hand-written word problems (pp. 1, 4).

Problems and their step-by-step solutions are generated algorithmically with SymPy and SciPy from randomly selected coefficients, functional forms and initial conditions, with no duplicates (pp. 2, 4).

A problem is included only if its approximate solution has less than 10% error from a numerically computed ground truth; HARDMATH-MINI is also checked visually by plotting analytical against numerical solutions (p5, p13).
The generated solution steps are not hand-checked: 'manually verifying each solution step-by-step is impractical for a dataset of this size' (p5).

Evaluation combines automatic checking of the boxed final answer (SymPy equivalence and numerical evaluation) with GPT-4o grading against the answer key, using rubrics adapted from course grading guidelines, for partial credit (p7; Table 5, p25).
The GPT-4o grading was checked by hand on an unspecified subset; average human adjustments per model and problem type range from -0.15 to +0.07 points (p7; Table 6, p26).
o1-mini with 5-shot chain-of-thought reaches 62.3% overall on HARDMATH-MINI and GPT-4 43.8% (p7; Table 2, p8); GPT-4 reaches 28.1% on the 40 word problems (p8).
The generation code can produce any number of additional problems (pp. 2, 10).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: instances generated by code from parameterised problem forms (pp. 2, 4); a code-generated step-by-step solution for every problem (pp. 4-5, 13-21); an automatic numerical validity gate on generated items (p5), comparable to EngTrace's deterministic Layer 0 gate; partial credit; a science-and-engineering motivation (p1). Lacks: an engineering domain (it is applied mathematics; only 40 hand-written word problems carry applied-science context, p6); step-level evaluation (the gold steps are never compared with model steps, and the GPT-4o rubrics grade regime-level answers with a single intermediate checkpoint for Laplace integrals, p25); hand-checked gold steps (p5); quantified validation of the evaluator against humans (p7, p26); and any contamination framing or private pool, since the evaluation set is a fixed public sample (p6).
notes: Naming: the paper writes HARDMATH in small capitals, the May reference title 'HARDMath', and the May text 'HardMath' (L157-158); the revised text should use 'HARDMath'. Internal inconsistencies in the paper: the open-source code model is 'CodeLlama-13b' in Table 2 and Table 7 but 'Codellama3-14b' in Table 6 (pp. 8, 26). The procedural grading (p7) also bears on the May introduction's claim that 'no existing benchmark verifies this process': HARDMath grades partly beyond the final answer, though with an LLM rubric judge and not by verification against gold steps. If the consolidator reads 'abstract' loosely (all mathematics benchmarks are abstract next to engineering), the verdict could fall to 'imprecise'; the omission of HARDMath's generator and gold solutions keeps it at 'misleading' in my reading.
